standard.title: Competing factors in design
standard.description: Explain how people in design and technologies occupations consider competing factors including sustainability in the design of products, services and environments
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can examine design and technologies occupations and factors including sustainability that impact on the design of products, services and environments (AC9TDE4K01). They have identified that designers consider multiple factors. They have not yet explained how competing factors are weighed against each other — the tension between them and how practitioners resolve it.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain how people in design and technologies occupations weigh competing factors including sustainability when designing products, services and environments, and identify examples of innovative solutions that resolve such tensions.

nodes.label: What competing factors means in design
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify that designers must weigh multiple factors that can pull in different directions, and name at least three factors that commonly compete
nodes.minimum_width: Name at least three factors a designer must consider (e.g. cost, sustainability, function, aesthetics, safety) and give one example where two factors pull in opposite directions
nodes.typical_width: Explain that design involves balancing competing factors that cannot all be maximised simultaneously; identify and describe how specific factors (aesthetics, function, sustainability, safety, cost) compete in a familiar product or service context
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australians considered competing factors in designing fish harvesting technologies — comparing selective harvesting techniques (fish traps, fish poisons allowing bycatch release) with high-yield non-selective methods like trawling
Investigate how Safety by Design principles (prevention, protection, proactive change) compete with other design factors such as cost and ease of use in a product or service context
Examine how engineers use biomimicry to resolve competing factors — finding a natural solution where function, sustainability and materials performance are already optimised

response_modes.reason: Students tend to treat factors as independent checklists rather than tensions. Multiple design contexts — each featuring a different pair of competing factors — help students see that the conflict between factors is the design problem, not just a constraint list.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The First Nations fish harvesting context is rich — it situates competing factors in a long-standing, evidence-based design tradition and creates direct comparison with modern industrial methods where sustainability was sacrificed. The biomimicry direction is also rich as a contemporary engineering context.
success_criteria: Names at least three factors that designers must consider
Explains at least one example where two factors conflict with each other
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify competing factors have no framework for design decision-making — every downstream capability (P01 investigation, P04 criteria negotiation, P03 material selection) requires reasoning through trade-offs. Without this, design decisions reduce to personal preference.

nodes.label: Sustainability as a competing factor
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how sustainability considerations compete with other design priorities and identify design decisions that resolve this tension
nodes.minimum_width: Describe one product, service or environment where sustainability was weighed against another factor, and explain what design decision was made
nodes.typical_width: Explain the sustainability implications of design decisions on local, regional and global communities; describe how designers resolve tension between sustainability and other priorities in at least two contexts (e.g. materials, energy, waste)
wider: Investigate the emergence of small businesses recycling materials (e.g. plastic tags and bottle tops into prosthetics) — explaining how they resolved the competition between cost, material availability, and sustainability

Evaluate a household product designed to reduce environmental impact (e.g. a solar-powered motor, a water-harvesting system, a boardwalk through fragile wetland) — identifying which competing factors the designer prioritised and which were deprioritised

Investigate the sustainability of a community service (e.g. Clean Up Australia Day in different communities) — assessing what factors contribute to its success and what sustainability risks or failures could occur

response_modes.reason: Sustainability is often treated as self-evidently good — students need contexts where it genuinely competes with something valuable (cost, performance, convenience) to understand it as a trade-off that designers actively negotiate rather than a principle they simply adopt.

success_criteria: Identifies a specific design decision where sustainability was weighed against another factor
Explains what the designer chose and why
